verses.summary: Moses is sent with signs and manifest authority.
verses.comparison_note: Commission and signs; Exodus details specific staff and hand signs absent from this ayah.

verses.summary: Moses is sent to Pharaoh and his chiefs; they follow Pharaoh's command, described as not rightly guided.
verses.comparison_note: Court opposition and Pharaoh's resistance; Exodus narrates encounters and hardening of heart, not the Qur'anic evaluation in these words.

verses.summary: Pharaoh leads his people on Resurrection Day into the Fire.
verses.comparison_note: Contrast: Exodus describes drowning at the sea, not Pharaoh leading people into eschatological Fire. Do not equate the two judgments.

verses.summary: A curse follows Pharaoh's people in this world and on the Resurrection Day.
verses.comparison_note: Only a loose judgment motif; no exact earlier two-stage curse text identified.

verses.summary: The passage transitions to reports of former towns, some still standing and others cut down.
verses.comparison_note: No source-specific earlier passage established for this retrospective formula.

dossier.title: Moses and Pharaoh: authority, following and judgment

sections.chronological_background: Exodus is an earlier Israelite textual tradition preserved through multiple textual witnesses. Date of literary composition, editorial development and surviving manuscripts must be handled separately; no witness was collated for this batch.

source_table.focus: Sea judgment, distinct from Qur'anic afterlife judgment

sections.similarities: Moses confronts Pharaoh, with signs and opposition; the ruler's conduct affects his followers.
sections.differences: Q11:98–99 gives eschatological consequences and a curse extending into the Resurrection; Exodus 14 describes a sea catastrophe, not this afterlife scene.
sections.transmission_and_dating: Hebrew Masoretic tradition, Septuagint and other witnesses require edition-specific comparison before publication; no manuscript dates verified in this batch.
sections.interpretations: Narrative inheritance, shared tradition and later theological reworking are research possibilities, not demonstrated transmission pathways.
